thread_tweets.text:
A startup or research team can run models on its own machine, keeping sensitive prompts and outputs on hardware it controls.

When the machine isn’t needed privately, the owner can put it into Earning mode and let B3IQ find paid work for it.

thread_tweets.full_text:

thread_tweets.text:
Owners keep 85% of what their machine earns. B3IQ takes the other 15% for finding the work and handling the marketplace side, which seems fair to me.

The catch is that a machine can’t earn and run private workloads at the same time, so you have to choose one or the other.

Earnings also depend on demand, so there’s no guaranteed monthly return.

🌍 MACRO: Yesterday’s US flash composite PMI jumped to 58.4, signalling the strongest business expansion since July 2021. Input costs also accelerated to a near four-year high. Strong growth plus stubborn inflation keeps further Fed tightening firmly in play.

☢️ URANIUM: Framatome has secured a commercial contract to supply a US reactor with fuel enriched above 5%, starting in 2028. The deal will extend operating cycles from 18 to 24 months. Another concrete investment in getting more reliable electricity from the existing nuclear fleet.

🥈 SILVER: Higher rate expectations are weighing on sentiment. The underlying supply challenge remains relevant: the Silver Institute’s April outlook projected a sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with mine production flat. A tight annual balance can coexist with sharp price corrections.

🔶 COPPER: Prysmian and Aurubis announced their largest-ever copper supply agreement yesterday, explicitly citing demand from power grids, electrification and AI infrastructure. Major industrial buyers are committing to long-term supply as electricity infrastructure expands.

🥇 GOLD: Further rate-hike expectations are keeping gold under pressure, while easing oil prices offer some relief. My read: sustained cooling in energy inflation could improve the setup by reducing pressure for additional tightening. The dollar and bond yields remain key signals to watch.

An intellectual argument for occasional use of Jew vs Zionist.  

1st, the Jews seem to be the only people who can demand that their name not be used. 

For example, the generic “white” people is often used to refer to colonizers, imperialists, and slavers. 

Yet millions of people of European ancestry cannot trace their family history to those activities. 

Is there strong evidence that the people of Estonia, for example, trafficked in these activities?

Moreover, even within an ethnic group, it was usually only a very small percentage that participated in these extreme activities. 

For example, the vast majority of men who fought and died on behalf of the Confederate States of America never owned slaves. Indeed, most were very poor. 

Thus, why is there this instance to make such a qualification between Jew and Zionist? 

I think it is clear. The government demands it.  

For example, if I say, “Whites owned slaves in the American South,” it is taken for granted that I don’t mean every single white man in the South owned slaves. Only that it was white men who owned slaves. 

Similarly, I should be able to say, “Jews are committing and supporting genocide.”  

That statement should not mean I believe every Jew is committing genocide insomuch as the earlier statement means every white man in the South had slaves. 

Every time I hear the word “Zionist” used, it just seems like a pussy ass excuse for saying Jew.

Let’s just treat all ethnic and race groups alike. In other words, be able to generalize from the whole in an understandable way.

One thing I’ve noticed: you can almost predict how well someone understands AI by how much time they spend on X.

You don’t even need to try every model yourself. You constantly see other people testing agents, computer use, biology, math, and random niche products.

At lunch I’ll mention a new AI product like Muse to someone who isn’t on X, and they’ll have no idea what I’m talking about. Meanwhile, everyone on X has seen what it can do and probably tried it already.

I keep doing this test and the correlation is kind of crazy. X is still the best place to understand what AI can actually do right now because so many AI researchers and builders are posting on the platform.

tweets.text:
Muse is winning at model-market fit. I haven’t seen anything it does today that ChatGPT Work couldn’t do months ago, or that Instinct or another agent couldn’t do. But using it feels different. It’s fast, smooth, and you actually want to keep using it.

A faster, cheaper model paired with a great harness makes a huge difference. For an agent taking dozens of steps to get something done, every bit of latency adds up. You feel it every time you ask for something and if it's too slow it will feel clunky and annoying.

And cost matters to the product experience too. It determines how much work you can afford to run in the background, how often the agent can check things, and how many attempts it can make. It's so obvious that they have a cheap model because they run the Feed updates hourly, they also create memories hourly too and not nightly like other agents. 

You can have the same capabilities on paper and end up with very different products. IMO that’s what I think Muse is getting right: the underlying model is very good.
